framing: Extract every character you retrieve, with its source intact
paragraphs: Retrieval failures often begin long before embeddings or ranking metrics run, inside document parsers that silently mangle numbers, drop headings, or mix page columns together. A model answering an LLM serving specification question looks fluent while returning the wrong timeout simply because the prefill timeout rule never survived extraction.

Across PDFs, HTML pages, scanned images, and Markdown files, the root cause takes a different technical form in each container. Native PDF streams position text glyphs by page coordinates and can interleave multi-column lines, OCR turns faint ink or skewed tables into lookalike characters such as 1S for 15, HTML tags split numbers across inline styling spans alongside navigation sidebars, and naive Markdown splitters slice inside fenced code blocks.

To make these failures concrete, this chapter follows an LLM inference serving specification (inference-spec-v3.pdf) paired with HTML API documentation, a scanned appendix page, and Markdown runtime notes. Whenever extraction introduces ambiguity, such as an uncertain OCR digit, encoding replacement marker, or out-of-order column, clean pipelines isolate the suspect extract for inspection rather than silently rewriting text before indexing.

By normalizing every parser path into one structured record schema carrying source locators, SHA-256 checksums, reading-order tags, and access permissions, teams ensure only checked evidence enters vector search and every later version diff can be audited cleanly.
outcomes: Diagnose format-specific extraction hazards across native PDFs, scanned OCR pages, HTML DOM trees, and Markdown code blocks using runnable Python adapters.
Normalize heterogeneous document outputs into one verified schema with stable source references, text digests, access tags, and explicit review gates before indexing.
Design visual page retrieval fallbacks and versioned re-indexing diffs that separate membership, wording, and permission changes cleanly.
question: If a scanned appendix page turns '15 seconds' into '1S seconds' during ingestion, why does holding the candidate for review outperform correcting '1S' to '15' automatically before retrieval?
